title: Ὁ Κοινὸς Γόος
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: This part opens the moment Menelaus's own long speech, left open at the end of odyssey-014, is confirmed to have closed, and Telemachus, overcome at the mention of his father, hides his tears behind his cloak. Menelaus notices and hesitates over what to do, until Helen enters and guesses at once that the young stranger must be Telemachus; Menelaus confirms it from the boy's likeness to Odysseus, and Peisistratus, Nestor's son, confirms it again. Menelaus's memories of Odysseus's own hardships, and his regret that the two of them never shared a home together, set the whole company weeping, and Peisistratus, remembering his own dead brother Antilochus, speaks about the small honors owed to the dead and asks that the weeping now be set aside. Menelaus agrees, praises Nestor's blessings in his sons, and turns the household from mourning to the supper still waiting for them; Asphalion pours water for their hands, and the meal begins.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τῷ δ’ ἄρα πατρὸς ὑφ’ ἵμερον ὦρσε γόοιο.
sentences.tr: hōs phato, tōi d’ ara patros hyph’ himeron ōrse gooio.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and in him then for his father it aroused a longing of lament.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and it stirred in him a longing to weep for his father.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο, 'so he spoke' (house table), is the poem's regular speech-closing formula: here it confirms that Menelaus's own long speech, left open at the end of odyssey-014 (4.78–112, ending "ὃν ἔλειπε νέον γεγαῶτ’ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ" with no closing quotation mark), has now finished — this line is narration, not a resumption of speech. ὑφ’ ... ὦρσε is tmesis: the preverb ὑπό, elided to ὑφ’, is split from ὦρσε (aorist of ὄρνυμι, 'stir up') by the intervening ἵμερον, together meaning 'aroused'. γόοιο is a genitive in -οιο (-ου) dependent on ἵμερον, 'a longing for lament'; πατρός is a further genitive, 'for his father'.

sentences.t:
δάκρυ δ’ ἀπὸ βλεφάρων χαμάδις βάλε πατρὸς ἀκούσας,
χλαῖναν πορφυρέην ἄντ’ ὀφθαλμοῖιν ἀνασχὼν
ἀμφοτέρῃσιν χερσί.
sentences.tr:
dakry d’ apo blepharōn chamadis bale patros akousas,
chlainan porphyreēn ant’ ophthalmoiin anaschōn
amphoterēisin chersi.
sentences.l:
And a tear from his eyelids to the ground he let fall, hearing of his father,
his purple cloak before his eyes having raised
with both hands.
sentences.i: And on hearing mention of his father he let a tear fall from his eyelids to the ground, raising his purple cloak before his eyes with both hands.
sentences.n: βάλε is the unaugmented aorist of βάλλω (Attic ἔβαλε), 'let fall'. ἀκούσας, an aorist participle of ἀκούω, takes the genitive πατρός, 'on hearing of his father' — the ordinary construction for verbs of perceiving. ὀφθαλμοῖιν is an epic dual dative, 'before his two eyes': Homer still marks the dual for paired body parts. ἀμφοτέρῃσιν is a dative plural in -ῃσι(ν) (Attic -αις) agreeing with χερσί. The gesture of hiding tears behind a raised cloak recurs almost verbatim at 4.153–154, when Menelaus does the same; see new-renderings.md for the fixed wording of the formula.

sentences.t:
νόησε δέ μιν Μενέλαος,
μερμήριξε δ’ ἔπειτα κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν,
ἠέ μιν αὐτὸν πατρὸς ἐάσειε μνησθῆναι
ἦ πρῶτ’ ἐξερέοιτο ἕκαστά τε πειρήσαιτο.
sentences.tr:
noēse de min Menelaos,
mermērixe d’ epeita kata phrena kai kata thymon,
ēe min auton patros easeie mnēsthēnai
ē prōt’ exereoito hekasta te peirēsaito.
sentences.l:
And Menelaus noticed him,
and then he pondered, in mind and in heart,
whether he should let him himself make mention of his father,
or should first question him and test him on each point.
sentences.i: And Menelaus noticed him, and then pondered in his mind and heart whether he should let him make mention of his father of his own accord, or should first question him and test him out on every point.
sentences.n: μερμήριξε is unaugmented (the root begins with a consonant, so Homer's optional augment simply is not added here). κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν is the house table's fixed 'in mind and in heart'. The two optatives ἐάσειε and ἐξερέοιτο/πειρήσαιτο set out a double indirect question ('whether ... or ...') in secondary sequence after the past-tense μερμήριξε, the ordinary Homeric construction for a deliberation reported in the past. μιν αὐτόν is emphatic, 'him, of his own accord'.

sentences.t:
ἧος ὁ ταῦθ’ ὥρμαινε κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν,
ἐκ δ’ Ἑλένη θαλάμοιο θυώδεος ὑψορόφοιο
ἤλυθεν Ἀρτέμιδι χρυσηλακάτῳ ἐικυῖα.
sentences.tr:
hēos ho tauth’ hōrmaine kata phrena kai kata thymon,
ek d’ Helenē thalamoio thyōdeos hypsorophoio
ēlythen Artemidi chrysēlakatōi eikuia.
sentences.l:
While he was pondering these things in mind and in heart,
out from her chamber, fragrant, high-roofed, came Helen,
like to Artemis of the golden distaff.
sentences.i: While he was turning this over in his mind and heart, Helen came out from her fragrant, high-roofed chamber, like Artemis of the golden distaff.
sentences.n: ἧος is the epic form of ἕως, 'while' (Attic ἕως); ταῦθ’ is ταῦτα, elided. ὥρμαινε is the augmented imperfect of ὁρμαίνω (ο→ω lengthening; the unaugmented Homeric form would be ὅρμαινε), a near-synonym of μερμηρίζω in the line before — Homer varies the verb but repeats the fixed formula κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν exactly. ὑψορόφοιο is a genitive in -οιο agreeing with θαλάμοιο; θυώδεος is a genitive in -εος (uncontracted, Attic -ους), the regular 3rd-declension ending, likewise agreeing with θαλάμοιο. ἐικυῖα is the feminine perfect participle of ἔοικα, 'resembling' (+ dat.). χρυσηλάκατος, 'of the golden distaff', is a standing epithet of Artemis, marking her among other things as patroness of women's indoor handiwork; logged as a likely-recurring formula in new-renderings.md.

sentences.t:
τῇ δ’ ἄρ’ ἅμ’ Ἀδρήστη κλισίην εὔτυκτον ἔθηκεν,
Ἀλκίππη δὲ τάπητα φέρεν μαλακοῦ ἐρίοιο,
sentences.tr:
tēi d’ ar’ ham’ Adrēstē klisiēn eutykton ethēken,
Alkippē de tapēta pheren malakou erioio,
sentences.l:
And with her then Adreste set a well-made seat,
and Alcippe brought a rug of soft wool,
sentences.i: And with her Adreste set out a well-made seat, and Alcippe brought a rug of soft wool,
sentences.n: This four-line sentence (123–127) runs past the four-line limit for a single tap-unit, so it is cut here at the comma where the syntax pauses most, between the first two handmaids' actions and the third's. ἔθηκεν is the augmented aorist of τίθημι, 'placed, set'; φέρεν is the unaugmented imperfect of φέρω, 'was bringing'. κλισίη here is 'seat, chair' in the general sense, kept distinct in translation from κλισμός at 4.136 (a chair proper, with a back). ἐρίοιο is a genitive in -οιο of ἔριον, epic εἶρος (cf. 4.135).

sentences.t:
Φυλὼ δ’ ἀργύρεον τάλαρον φέρε, τόν οἱ ἔθηκεν
Ἀλκάνδρη, Πολύβοιο δάμαρ, ὃς ἔναι’ ἐνὶ Θήβῃς
Αἰγυπτίῃς, ὅθι πλεῖστα δόμοις ἐν κτήματα κεῖται·
sentences.tr:
Phylō d’ argyreon talaron phere, ton hoi ethēken
Alkandrē, Polyboio damar, hos enai’ eni Thēbēis
Aigyptiēis, hothi pleista domois en ktēmata keitai·
sentences.i: and Phylo brought a silver basket, which Alcandre, wife of Polybus, had given her — Polybus, who lived in Egyptian Thebes, where the greatest store of wealth lies in men's houses;
sentences.n: ὅς is masculine and so refers back to Πολύβοιο rather than to the nearer Ἀλκάνδρη: it is Polybus, not his wife, who lived in Thebes. ἔναι(ε) is the imperfect of ναίω 'dwell', its augment showing as a plain ἐ- before the consonant-initial stem ναι-. This is Egyptian Thebes (Θῆβαι Αἰγύπτιαι), the city of a hundred gates, which Homer keeps distinct from Boeotian Thebes; its proverbial wealth is stated outright by πλεῖστα κτήματα, 'the most treasures'.

sentences.t:
ὃς Μενελάῳ δῶκε δύ’ ἀργυρέας ἀσαμίνθους,
δοιοὺς δὲ τρίποδας, δέκα δὲ χρυσοῖο τάλαντα.
sentences.tr:
hos Menelaōi dōke dy’ argyreas asaminthous,
doious de tripodas, deka de chrysoio talanta.
sentences.l:
who to Menelaus gave two silver baths,
and two tripods, and ten talents of gold.
sentences.i: who gave Menelaus two silver baths, two tripods, and ten talents of gold.
sentences.n: δοιούς is a poetic alternative to δύο (both words for 'two' stand within two lines, δύ’ in 128 and δοιούς in 129, a simple metrical variation). τάλαντον is a unit of weight, not a coin: Homeric wealth is reckoned in weighed gold, minted currency belonging to a later age. ἀσάμινθος, 'bath, bathing-tub', is the word already met at 3.468 (Telemachus stepping from his bath), here plural for the two vessels given as gifts.

sentences.t: χωρὶς δ’ αὖθ’ Ἑλένῃ ἄλοχος πόρε κάλλιμα δῶρα·
sentences.tr: chōris d’ auth’ Helenēi alochos pore kallima dōra·
sentences.l: And apart, in turn, to Helen his wife gave beautiful gifts;
sentences.i: And separately, his wife gave Helen beautiful gifts of her own;
sentences.n: χωρίς marks these as gifts given apart from what Polybus gave Menelaus. ἄλοχος here is Alcandre, 'his wife', i.e. Polybus's, returning to the subject introduced by δάμαρ two lines earlier. πόρε is the aorist of the defective verb πόρω, 'furnish, grant', found only in the aorist. κάλλιμος is a poetic by-form of καλός, 'beautiful', with the productive Homeric suffix -ιμος.

sentences.t:
χρυσέην τ’ ἠλακάτην τάλαρόν θ’ ὑπόκυκλον ὄπασσεν
ἀργύρεον, χρυσῷ δ’ ἐπὶ χείλεα κεκράαντο.
sentences.tr:
chryseēn t’ ēlakatēn talaron th’ hypokyklon opassen
argyreon, chrysōi d’ epi cheilea kekraanto.
sentences.l:
a golden distaff she gave, and a basket running on wheels,
of silver, and with gold upon the rims it was finished.
sentences.i: she gave her a golden distaff and a basket running on wheels, of silver, its rims finished with gold.
sentences.n: ὄπασσεν is the aorist of ὀπάζω, 'grant, bestow', often used of gift-giving. ὑπόκυκλος, 'running on wheels beneath', describes a basket set on a small wheeled stand so that it could be rolled to hand — a realistic domestic detail. ἀργύρεον, held over from line 131 by enjambment, agrees with τάλαρον. κεκράανται is the Homeric perfect passive of κραίνω, 'accomplish, finish' (Attic κέκρανται); χρυσῷ is a dative of means, 'in gold, with gold'.

sentences.t:
τόν ῥά οἱ ἀμφίπολος Φυλὼ παρέθηκε φέρουσα
νήματος ἀσκητοῖο βεβυσμένον·
sentences.tr:
ton rha hoi amphipolos Phylō parethēke pherousa
nēmatos askētoio bebysmenon·
sentences.l:
which then for her the handmaid Phylo set down, bringing it,
filled with well-spun yarn;
sentences.i: which the handmaid Phylo brought and set down for her, filled with well-spun yarn;
sentences.n: βεβυσμένον is a perfect passive participle of βύω, 'stuff, cram full', agreeing with τόν (the basket, τάλαρον). νήματος ἀσκητοῖο is a genitive of content, 'with yarn'; ἀσκητός, from ἀσκέω 'work skilfully', is 'wrought, well-worked'. παρέθηκε φέρουσα, a finite aorist with a present participle of manner, is the common idiom 'she brought and set it down', the participle describing the accompanying action of carrying.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ
ἠλακάτη τετάνυστο ἰοδνεφὲς εἶρος ἔχουσα.
sentences.tr:
autar ep’ autōi
ēlakatē tetanysto iodnephes eiros echousa.
sentences.l:
but upon it
the distaff was laid, holding violet-dark wool.
sentences.i: and on top of it lay the distaff, holding wool of a violet-dark hue.
sentences.n: τετάνυστο is a pluperfect passive of τανύω 'stretch, lay out', with imperfect force in Homer ('lay stretched'), agreeing with ἠλακάτη. ἰοδνεφής, 'dark as a violet' (ἴον + the root of δνόφος 'darkness'), has an exact shade that is uncertain, though 'dusky violet-purple' is the generally accepted sense. εἶρος is the epic form of ἔριον 'wool' (cf. μαλακοῦ ἐρίοιο at 4.124).

sentences.t: ἕζετο δ’ ἐν κλισμῷ, ὑπὸ δὲ θρῆνυς ποσὶν ἦεν.
sentences.tr: hezeto d’ en klismōi, hypo de thrēnys posin ēen.
sentences.l: And she sat down on a chair, and beneath, a footstool was for her feet.
sentences.i: And she sat down on a chair, with a footstool beneath her feet.
sentences.n: κλισμός is the ordinary word for a chair with a back, kept distinct here from κλισίη at 4.123, a more general 'seat', though the underlying pieces of furniture may not have differed greatly — English can keep the two Greek nouns apart even where the objects were similar. ἦεν is the epic form of ἦν, 'was' (cf. 1.18). θρῆνυς, a footstool, regularly stood beneath a seated figure's feet, a detail of aristocratic furnishing.

sentences.t: αὐτίκα δ’ ἥ γ’ ἐπέεσσι πόσιν ἐρέεινεν ἕκαστα·
sentences.tr: autika d’ hē g’ epeessi posin ereeinen hekasta·
sentences.l: And at once she, with words, was questioning her husband on each point;
sentences.i: And at once she began questioning her husband about every particular.
sentences.n: ἐρέεινεν, an imperfect of ἐρεείνω, has inceptive or durative force, 'began to question, kept questioning'; ἕκαστα is its second accusative, 'about each thing'. ἐπέεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι, from ἔπος 'word' (cf. ἔπε’ at 1.38). This narrator's line announces the coming speech without quoting it; Helen's actual words begin only with the next line, which is why the following unit, not this one, carries the mark for her speech.

sentences.t:
ἴδμεν δή, Μενέλαε διοτρεφές, οἵ τινες οἵδε
ἀνδρῶν εὐχετόωνται ἱκανέμεν ἡμέτερον δῶ;
sentences.tr:
idmen dē, Menelae diotrephes, hoi tines hoide
andrōn euchetoōntai hikanemen hēmeteron dō;
sentences.l:
“Do we know, then, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured, who these here,
of men, declare themselves, to have come to our house?
sentences.i: “Do we know yet, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured, who these men are who claim to have come to our house?
sentences.n: διοτρεφές is a vocative of διοτρεφής, 'Zeus-nurtured', the epithet already fixed for kings in the house table's διοτρεφέες βασιλῆες, here applied singly to Menelaus, as again at 4.156. οἵ τινες, 'who indeed', is an indirect question with the indefinite relative. εὐχετόωνται is a diectasis form (Attic εὔχονται) of εὔχομαι, 'declare, claim to be'. ἱκανέμεν is an epic infinitive in -έμεν of ἱκάνω, 'arrive'.

sentences.t: ψεύσομαι ἦ ἔτυμον ἐρέω;
sentences.tr: pseusomai ē etymon ereō;
sentences.l: Shall I speak falsely, or shall I say what is true?
sentences.i: Shall I be lying, or shall I say what is true?
sentences.n: ψεύσομαι and ἐρέω are both futures used deliberatively, a rhetorical self-questioning familiar from Attic too (the deliberative future or subjunctive). ἔτυμον, 'true, real', is used adverbially, the neuter accusative of ἐτυμός, related to the ἐτήτυμον already met at 4.140's near environs and in the house table's ἀτρεκέως κατάλεξον line.

sentences.t: κέλεται δέ με θυμός.
sentences.tr: keletai de me thymos.
sentences.l: And my heart bids me speak.
sentences.i: But my heart urges me to speak.
sentences.n: κέλεται is the present of κέλομαι, 'bid, urge', with θυμός as subject and the accusative με as object — an idiom in which the heart, not the person, does the urging, as often in Homer's language of the inner life. The short sentence answers Helen's own hesitation in the line before with a plain statement of resolve.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ πώ τινά φημι ἐοικότα ὧδε ἰδέσθαι
οὔτ’ ἄνδρ’ οὔτε γυναῖκα, σέβας μ’ ἔχει εἰσορόωσαν,
ὡς ὅδ’ Ὀδυσσῆος μεγαλήτορος υἷι ἔοικε,
sentences.tr:
ou gar pō tina phēmi eoikota hōde idesthai
out’ andr’ oute gynaika, sebas m’ echei eisoroōsan,
hōs hod’ Odyssēos megalētoros huii eoike,
sentences.l:
For I say that never yet have I seen anyone so like —
neither man nor woman (wonder holds me as I look on) —
as this one is like the son of great-hearted Odysseus,
sentences.i: For I declare I have never yet seen anyone, man or woman, so like — wonder holds me as I gaze — as this man is like the son of great-hearted Odysseus,
sentences.n: This sentence runs 141–146, past the four-line limit, so it is cut here at the comma before the name Τηλεμάχῳ is given in apposition. φημί means 'declare, assert' rather than 'think'. πώ with the negative is 'never yet'. σέβας, 'awe, wonder', is subject of ἔχει, with the participle εἰσορόωσαν (feminine, agreeing with the unexpressed 'me', Helen) describing her attendant action, 'as I gaze'. μεγαλήτορος is a genitive in -ος agreeing with Ὀδυσσῆος (double-σ, a metrical variant of Ὀδυσῆος).

sentences.t:
Τηλεμάχῳ, τὸν ἔλειπε νέον γεγαῶτ’ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ
κεῖνος ἀνήρ, ὅτ’ ἐμεῖο κυνώπιδος εἵνεκ’ Ἀχαιοὶ
ἤλθεθ’ ὑπὸ Τροίην πόλεμον θρασὺν ὁρμαίνοντες.
sentences.tr:
Tēlemachōi, ton eleipe neon gegaōt’ eni oikōi
keinos anēr, hot’ emeio kynōpidos heinek’ Achaioi
ēltheth’ hypo Troiēn polemon thrasyn hormainontes.
sentences.l:
Telemachus, whom that man left newly-born in the house
— that man — when, for my sake, dog-faced as I am, you Achaeans
came beneath Troy, pondering bold war.”
sentences.i: Telemachus, whom that man left as a newborn in the house, when, because of me, shameless as I was, you Achaeans came to Troy, intent on grim war.”
sentences.n: κυνῶπις, 'dog-faced, dog-eyed' (κύων + ὤψ), is Helen's standing self-reproach, since the dog was proverbially shameless in Greek thought; logged as a likely-recurring formula in new-renderings.md. εἵνεκα (Attic ἕνεκα) governs the epic genitive ἐμεῖο (Attic ἐμοῦ). ἤλθεθ’ is ἤλθετε, second-person plural, elided and aspirated before ὑπό — a striking shift from the third-person Ἀχαιοί just named to direct second-person address, a rare Homeric 'apostrophe' extended here to a whole army rather than a single hero. ὁρμαίνοντες echoes ὥρμαινε at 4.120: the deliberation that was Menelaus's own private thought now becomes the Achaeans' collective resolve for war. This closes Helen's speech.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη ξανθὸς Μενέλαος·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ apameibomenos prosephē xanthos Menelaos·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed fair-haired Menelaus:
sentences.i: In answer fair-haired Menelaus said to her:
sentences.n: This is the fixed reply-formula τὴν/τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη (house table), kept deliberately distinct in translation from the other reply-formula τὸν/τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα. ξανθὸς Μενέλαος, 'fair-haired Menelaus', is his standing epithet-name pair, used again to introduce his replies at 4.168 and 4.203. τήν is the accusative pronoun 'her', object of προσέφη, referring to Helen. This is narration, not yet the speech itself; Menelaus's actual words begin only with the next line, which is why that unit, not this one, carries the mark and the opening quotation mark (the same principle already applied at 4.137).

sentences.t: οὕτω νῦν καὶ ἐγὼ νοέω, γύναι, ὡς σὺ ἐίσκεις·
sentences.tr: houtō nyn kai egō noeō, gynai, hōs sy eiskeis·
sentences.l: “So now I too think, wife, as you guess;
sentences.i: “So I too now think, wife, just as you guess;
sentences.n: γύναι is the vocative of γυνή, used here as 'wife' (Menelaus to Helen) rather than the generic 'woman'. ἐίσκεις is the present of ἐΐσκω, 'liken, guess, conjecture'. νοέω, 'perceive, form a judgment', answers Helen's own uncertain ψεύσομαι ἦ ἔτυμον ἐρέω with a matching verb of the mind. οὕτω ... ὡς frames Menelaus's agreement as an exact match to Helen's guess.

sentences.t:
κείνου γὰρ τοιοίδε πόδες τοιαίδε τε χεῖρες
ὀφθαλμῶν τε βολαὶ κεφαλή τ’ ἐφύπερθέ τε χαῖται.
sentences.tr:
keinou gar toioide podes toiaide te cheires
ophthalmōn te bolai kephalē t’ ephyperthe te chaitai.
sentences.l:
For such are that man's feet, and such the hands,
and the glances of the eyes, and the head, and above it, the hair.
sentences.i: For such are his feet, such his hands, the glances of his eyes, his head, and the hair above it — just as that man's were.
sentences.n: βολαί, from βάλλω, literally 'castings, throws', here 'glances' — the eyes are pictured as casting looks outward. ἐφύπερθε, 'from above, on top', governs χαῖται loosely, 'the hair on top of the head'. τοιόσδε/τοιάδε, 'such, of this kind', correlates implicitly with κείνου, 'that man' (Odysseus), a genitive of comparison. Menelaus lists four points of physical resemblance — feet, hands, eyes, hair — a catalogue typical of Homeric recognition scenes.

sentences.t:
καὶ νῦν ἦ τοι ἐγὼ μεμνημένος ἀμφ’ Ὀδυσῆι
μυθεόμην, ὅσα κεῖνος ὀιζύσας ἐμόγησεν
ἀμφ’ ἐμοί, αὐτὰρ ὁ πικρὸν ὑπ’ ὀφρύσι δάκρυον εἶβε,
χλαῖναν πορφυρέην ἄντ’ ὀφθαλμοῖιν ἀνασχών.
sentences.tr:
kai nyn ē toi egō memnēmenos amph’ Odysēi
mytheomēn, hosa keinos oizysas emogēsen
amph’ emoi, autar ho pikron hyp’ ophrysi dakryon eibe,
chlainan porphyreēn ant’ ophthalmoiin anaschōn.
sentences.l:
And now indeed I, mindful of Odysseus,
was telling all that he, suffering hardship, toiled
on my account; but he let flow a bitter tear beneath his brows,
his purple cloak before his eyes having raised.”
sentences.i: And just now I myself, with Odysseus in mind, was telling of all the hardship and toil he bore on my account; but he let a bitter tear fall beneath his brows, raising his purple cloak before his eyes.”
sentences.n: μεμνημένος, a participle of μιμνήσκομαι that usually governs a bare genitive, here instead takes ἀμφ’ Ὀδυσῆι, 'about Odysseus' — a Homeric periphrasis with ἀμφί + dative in place of the genitive of the thing remembered. ὀιζύσας is an aorist participle of ὀϊζύω, 'suffer misery, toil in wretchedness', agreeing with κεῖνος. εἶβε, 'let flow, shed' (of tears), is a rare poetic verb. ὀφρύσι is a dative plural in -υσι, from ὀφρύς 'eyebrow'. The last line repeats 4.115 exactly (see new-renderings.md) — the same gesture of hiding tears behind a raised cloak, now performed by Menelaus as Telemachus did moments before.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Νεστορίδης Πεισίστρατος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ au Nestoridēs Peisistratos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: Him then in turn spoke Peisistratus, Nestor's son, face to face:
sentences.i: Then Peisistratus, son of Nestor, spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This reply-formula follows the pattern already fixed in the house table for τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Εὐρύμαχος Πολύβου πάϊς ἀντίον ηὔδα and τὸν δ’ Εὐηνορίδης Λειώκριτος ἀντίον ηὔδα: name and patronymic fill the line, closing with ἀντίον ηὔδα, 'spoke face to face'. αὖ is a shorter form of αὖτε, 'in turn'; Νεστορίδης, 'son of Nestor', is a patronymic in the common -ίδης suffix. Logged in new-renderings.md, as this particular name-filling is new to this part. This is narration, not the speech itself; the mark and opening quotation mark belong on the next unit, where Peisistratus's actual words begin.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη Μενέλαε διοτρεφές, ὄρχαμε λαῶν,
κείνου μέν τοι ὅδ’ υἱὸς ἐτήτυμον, ὡς ἀγορεύεις·
sentences.tr:
Atreïdē Menelae diotrephes, orchame laōn,
keinou men toi hod’ huios etētymon, hōs agoreueis·
sentences.l:
“Atreus' son, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured, chief of the people,
that man's son, truly, is this one, as you declare;
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured, chief of the people, this is indeed that man's son, truly, as you say;
sentences.n: The whole line 156 is a formal vocative, combining the patronymic Ἀτρεΐδη (the house table's 'Atreus' son', there of Agamemnon, here of his brother, since both were sons of Atreus), the epithet διοτρεφές already met at 4.138, and ὄρχαμε λαῶν, 'chief of the people' — a variant of the table's fixed ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν, 'chief of men', with λαός 'host, people' in place of ἀνήρ. τοι is the affirming particle 'truly, you know', not the enclitic 'to you'. ἐτήτυμον is used adverbially, 'truly, in fact'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σαόφρων ἐστί, νεμεσσᾶται δ’ ἐνὶ θυμῷ
ὧδ’ ἐλθὼν τὸ πρῶτον ἐπεσβολίας ἀναφαίνειν
ἄντα σέθεν, τοῦ νῶι θεοῦ ὣς τερπόμεθ’ αὐδῇ.
sentences.tr:
alla saophrōn esti, nemessatai d’ eni thymōi
hōd’ elthōn to prōton epesbolias anaphainein
anta sethen, tou nōi theou hōs terpometh’ audēi.
sentences.l:
but he is self-possessed, and feels shame in his heart
at coming here for the first time, to show forth reckless words
before you, whose voice we two delight in, as in a god's.
sentences.i: but he is self-possessed, and it shames his heart, coming here for the first time, to blurt out rash words in front of you, whose voice the two of us delight in as if it were a god's.
sentences.n: σαόφρων is the epic/Ionic by-form (long α, uncontracted) of σώφρων, 'temperate, self-controlled' — rendered 'self-possessed' here rather than 'sound-minded' to avoid collision with the already house-fixed ἐχέφρων Πηνελόπεια, 'sound-minded Penelope' (4.111), a distinct φρήν-compound the table keeps separate. νεμεσσᾶται is a deponent middle, 'feels indignation, is ashamed', governing the infinitive ἀναφαίνειν. ἐπεσβολίας, 'words thrown out rashly' (ἔπος + βάλλω), is a rare compound found only here in Homer. σέθεν is the epic genitive of σύ (Attic σοῦ); νῶι is the dual 'we two' (Telemachus and Peisistratus).

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐμὲ προέηκε Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ
τῷ ἅμα πομπὸν ἕπεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
autar eme proeēke Gerēnios hippota Nestōr
tōi hama pompon hepesthai·
sentences.l:
but me the Gerenian horseman Nestor sent forth,
to go with him as his escort;
sentences.i: but the Gerenian horseman Nestor sent me along with him, as his companion on the road;
sentences.n: Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ is Nestor's fixed name-title (house table, 3.68), unchanged here. προέηκε is the aorist of προΐημι, 'send forth'. πομπὸν ἕπεσθαι, literally 'to follow as an escort', is an epexegetic infinitive giving the purpose of the sending; τῷ ἅμα, 'along with him', refers back to Telemachus.

sentences.t:
ἐέλδετο γάρ σε ἰδέσθαι,
ὄφρα οἱ ἤ τι ἔπος ὑποθήσεαι ἠέ τι ἔργον.
sentences.tr:
eeldeto gar se idesthai,
ophra hoi ē ti epos hypothēseai ēe ti ergon.
sentences.l:
for he was longing to see you,
so that to him either some word you might suggest, or some deed.
sentences.i: for he was longing to see you, so that you might counsel him with some word or some deed.
sentences.n: ἐέλδετο, an unaugmented imperfect of ἐέλδομαι, 'desire, long for', shows the reduplicated epic present stem. ὑποθήσεαι is a future indicative used within an ὄφρα purpose clause where a subjunctive might be expected, an idiom that lends the hoped-for outcome extra certainty. ἔπος ... ἔργον, 'word ... deed', is a common Homeric pairing for counsel that is both spoken advice and practical help.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ γὰρ ἄλγε’ ἔχει πατρὸς πάϊς οἰχομένοιο
ἐν μεγάροις, ᾧ μὴ ἄλλοι ἀοσσητῆρες ἔωσιν,
ὡς νῦν Τηλεμάχῳ ὁ μὲν οἴχεται, οὐδέ οἱ ἄλλοι
εἴσ’ οἵ κεν κατὰ δῆμον ἀλάλκοιεν κακότητα.
sentences.tr:
polla gar alge’ echei patros païs oichomenoio
en megarois, hōi mē alloi aossētēres eōsin,
hōs nyn Tēlemachōi ho men oichetai, oude hoi alloi
eis’ hoi ken kata dēmon alalkoien kakotēta.
sentences.l:
For many pains has the son of a departed father,
in the halls, for whom no other helpers there may be,
as now for Telemachus: he is gone, nor for him are there others
who might ward off, throughout the land, misery.”
sentences.i: For a son whose father is gone has many griefs in the halls, when there are no other helpers for him, as now with Telemachus: his father is gone, and he has no others who might ward off trouble throughout the land.”
sentences.n: πάϊς οἰχομένοιο πατρός, 'the son of a father who is gone', is a general reflection Peisistratus applies as much to his own case as to Telemachus's — his own dead brother Antilochus is named at 4.187. ἀοσσητῆρες, 'helpers, defenders', is a rare noun. ἔωσιν is a present subjunctive of εἰμί in a general relative clause. ἀλάλκοιεν is a reduplicated aorist optative of the root of ἀλέξω, 'ward off', governing κακότητα. οἴχεται (166) is a vivid present with perfect force, 'he is gone' — repeating the verb of 4.164's general maxim in Telemachus's own particular case.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη ξανθὸς Μενέλαος·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē xanthos Menelaos·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed fair-haired Menelaus:
sentences.i: In answer fair-haired Menelaus said to him:
sentences.n: The same fixed reply-formula as 4.147, now with the masculine pronoun τόν (Peisistratus) in place of the feminine τήν (Helen). See the note at 4.147 for the formula's deliberate distinction from τὸν/τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα. This is narration, not the speech itself; the mark and opening quotation mark belong on the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι, ἦ μάλα δὴ φίλου ἀνέρος υἱὸς ἐμὸν δῶ
ἵκεθ’, ὃς εἵνεκ’ ἐμεῖο πολέας ἐμόγησεν ἀέθλους·
sentences.tr:
ō popoi, ē mala dē philou aneros huios emon dō
hiketh’, hos heinek’ emeio poleas emogēsen aethlous·
sentences.l:
“Ah! Truly, indeed, the son of a dear man to my house
has come — he who for my sake toiled through many trials;
sentences.i: “Ah, truly the son of a dear friend has come to my house — a man who toiled through many trials for my sake;
sentences.n: ὢ πόποι is the fixed exclamation of the house table (1.32). ἦ μάλα δή stacks three particles of emphasis, 'truly indeed, in fact'. ἵκεθ’ is ἵκετο, the unaugmented aorist middle of ἱκνέομαι, 'arrive'. πολέας is the epic accusative plural of πολύς (Attic πολλούς). ἀέθλους, uncontracted for ἄθλους, are the 'trials' of the Trojan War, fought nominally for Menelaus's own sake, to recover Helen.

sentences.t:
καί μιν ἔφην ἐλθόντα φιλησέμεν ἔξοχον ἄλλων
Ἀργείων, εἰ νῶιν ὑπεὶρ ἅλα νόστον ἔδωκε
νηυσὶ θοῇσι γενέσθαι Ὀλύμπιος εὐρύοπα Ζεύς.
sentences.tr:
kai min ephēn elthonta philēsemen exochon allōn
Argeiōn, ei nōin hypeir hala noston edōke
nēusi thoēisi genesthai Olympios euryopa Zeus.
sentences.l:
and I said that I would cherish him, on his coming, beyond others
of the Argives, if to us two, over the sea, a homecoming
with swift ships, Olympian, far-thundering Zeus had granted to come to pass.
sentences.i: and I said that, if he came, I would cherish him above all other Argives, if only Olympian Zeus who thunders from afar had granted the two of us a homecoming over the sea in our swift ships.
sentences.n: φιλησέμεν is a future infinitive in -έμεν (Attic φιλήσειν), object of ἔφην. νῶιν is the dual dative, 'to us two', Menelaus and Odysseus. νηυσὶ θοῇσι reuses the house table's fixed 'swift ship', here plural. εὐρύοπα Ζεύς is the house table's fixed 'far-thundering Zeus'. The whole wish is unreal: Menelaus imagines a joint homecoming that in fact never happened, since Odysseus never returned from Troy at all, let alone travelled home together with him.

sentences.t:
καί κέ οἱ Ἄργεϊ νάσσα πόλιν καὶ δώματ’ ἔτευξα,
ἐξ Ἰθάκης ἀγαγὼν σὺν κτήμασι καὶ τέκεϊ ᾧ
καὶ πᾶσιν λαοῖσι, μίαν πόλιν ἐξαλαπάξας,
αἳ περιναιετάουσιν, ἀνάσσονται δ’ ἐμοὶ αὐτῷ.
sentences.tr:
kai ke hoi Argeï nassa polin kai dōmat’ eteuxa,
ex Ithakēs agagōn syn ktēmasi kai tekeï hōi
kai pasin laoisi, mian polin exalapaxas,
hai perinaietaousin, anassontai d’ emoi autōi.
sentences.l:
and I would have settled him a city in Argos, and built a house,
bringing him from Ithaca with his possessions and his own child
and all his people, having emptied out one city
of those that dwell around, and are ruled by me myself.
sentences.i: and I would have settled him with a city in Argos and built him a house, bringing him from Ithaca with his goods and his own child and all his people, after emptying out one of the cities round about that are ruled by me myself.
sentences.n: νάσσα is the aorist of ναίω used causatively, 'settled, gave a place to dwell' — distinct from the intransitive ἔναιε, 'dwelt', at 4.126. τέκεϊ ᾧ is the possessive ὅς, ἥ, ὅν, 'his own child' (Telemachus). ἐξαλαπάξας, from ἐξαλαπάζω, 'sack, empty out utterly', is the same violent verb used of sacking Troy, here applied startlingly to Menelaus's own subject cities, emptied simply to make room for a friend. περιναιετάουσιν is an uncontracted epic present, 'lie round about, are situated nearby'.

sentences.t: καί κε θάμ’ ἐνθάδ’ ἐόντες ἐμισγόμεθ’·
sentences.tr: kai ke tham’ enthad’ eontes emisgometh’·
sentences.l: and often, being here, we would have mingled with one another;
sentences.i: and, living here, we would often have been together;
sentences.n: κε with the imperfect ἐμισγόμεθα (rather than an aorist or future) marks an unreal, counterfactual condition continuing from νάσσα, ἔτευξα in the sentence before: Menelaus is describing what would have happened, not what did. ἐόντες is the present participle of εἰμί, 'being'. ἐμισγόμεθα, middle of μίσγω, is 'mix, associate, keep company'; θάμα is 'often, again and again'.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ κεν ἡμέας
ἄλλο διέκρινεν φιλέοντέ τε τερπομένω τε,
πρίν γ’ ὅτε δὴ θανάτοιο μέλαν νέφος ἀμφεκάλυψεν.
sentences.tr:
oude ken hēmeas
allo diekrinen phileonte te terpomenō te,
prin g’ hote dē thanatoio melan nephos amphekalypsen.
sentences.l:
and nothing else would have parted us, the two of us,
loving and delighting in each other,
until the black cloud of death had covered us about.
sentences.i: and nothing else would have parted us as we loved and took pleasure in each other, until the black cloud of death had closed over us.
sentences.n: φιλέοντέ and τερπομένω are dual participles (agreeing with the unexpressed ἡμέας, 'us two'), a number largely lost outside epic. διέκρινεν shows its augment as an elided vowel behind the prefixed preposition διά (δι’ ἔκρινεν), the pattern noted in the conventions for tmesis-adjacent forms. θανάτοιο μέλαν νέφος, 'the black cloud of death', is a vivid Homeric metaphor for the moment of dying, pictured as an engulfing darkness.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ τὰ μέν που μέλλεν ἀγάσσεσθαι θεὸς αὐτός,
ὃς κεῖνον δύστηνον ἀνόστιμον οἶον ἔθηκεν.
sentences.tr:
alla ta men pou mellen agassesthai theos autos,
hos keinon dystēnon anostimon oion ethēken.
sentences.l:
But these things, it seems, a god himself was destined to begrudge,
who made that wretched man alone without return.”
sentences.i: But it seems some god himself was bound to grudge us this, the god who made that unhappy man alone without a homecoming.”
sentences.n: ἀγάσσεσθαι is the future infinitive middle of ἄγαμαι, 'feel envy, grudge, resent' — the recurring Homeric idea that a god may resent mortal happiness carried too far. που, 'somewhere, presumably', softens the claim into a guess. ἀνόστιμον, 'without a return', is built on the root of the fixed νόστιμον ἦμαρ (house table) but negated with ἀν-. οἶον here is 'alone' (smooth breathing), stressing that of all the returning Achaeans Odysseus alone was denied his homecoming. This closes Menelaus's second speech.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τοῖσι δὲ πᾶσιν ὑφ’ ἵμερον ὦρσε γόοιο.
sentences.tr: hōs phato, toisi de pasin hyph’ himeron ōrse gooio.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and in them all it aroused a longing for lament.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and it stirred in all of them a longing to weep.
sentences.n: This line echoes 4.113 almost exactly, but where that line had τῷ ... πατρός ('in him, for his father', of Telemachus alone), this one has τοῖσι ... πᾶσιν ('in them, all of them'): the grief that began privately in Telemachus at the mention of his father now spreads to the whole company at the end of Menelaus's own speech. See the note at 4.113 for ὑφ’ ... ὦρσε as tmesis. πᾶσιν is dative plural, ν-movable.

sentences.t:
κλαῖε μὲν Ἀργείη Ἑλένη, Διὸς ἐκγεγαυῖα,
κλαῖε δὲ Τηλέμαχός τε καὶ Ἀτρεΐδης Μενέλαος,
οὐδ’ ἄρα Νέστορος υἱὸς ἀδακρύτω ἔχεν ὄσσε·
sentences.tr:
klaie men Argeiē Helenē, Dios ekgegauia,
klaie de Tēlemachos te kai Atreïdēs Menelaos,
oud’ ara Nestoros huios adakrytō echen osse·
sentences.i: Argive Helen wept, the daughter sprung from Zeus, and Telemachus wept, and Menelaus, son of Atreus, and Nestor's son too did not keep his eyes free of tears;
sentences.n: Διὸς ἐκγεγαυῖα, 'sprung of Zeus', is a new formula for Helen (see new-renderings.md), built on the perfect participle of ἐκγίγνομαι and kept distinct from the house table's Διὸς θυγάτηρ, 'daughter of Zeus', used of Athena. κλαῖε μέν ... κλαῖε δέ repeats the verb anaphorically for each mourner in turn. ὄσσε is the epic dual, 'the two eyes' (Attic ὄμματα), with the dual adjective ἀδακρύτω agreeing, 'tearless'. ἔχεν is the unaugmented imperfect of ἔχω.

sentences.t:
μνήσατο γὰρ κατὰ θυμὸν ἀμύμονος Ἀντιλόχοιο,
τόν ῥ’ Ἠοῦς ἔκτεινε φαεινῆς ἀγλαὸς υἱός·
sentences.tr:
mnēsato gar kata thymon amymonos Antilochoio,
ton rh’ Ēous ekteine phaeinēs aglaos huios·
sentences.l:
for he called to mind in his heart blameless Antilochus,
whom the splendid son of shining Dawn had slain;
sentences.i: for in his heart he remembered blameless Antilochus, whom the splendid son of shining Dawn had killed;
sentences.n: ἀμύμων is the house table's fixed 'blameless' (etymology disputed, see the note at 1.29), here of Antilochus, Peisistratus's own brother. μνήσατο is the unaugmented aorist middle of μιμνήσκομαι + genitive, as already at 1.29 of Aegisthus. ὁ Ἠοῦς ... ἀγλαὸς υἱός, 'the splendid son of shining Dawn', is a periphrasis for Memnon, the Ethiopian king and son of the dawn-goddess Eos, who killed Antilochus at Troy and was himself slain by Achilles — a story assumed known, not narrated here. ἀγλαός is the house table's fixed 'splendid' (φαίδιμος is reserved for 'glorious').

sentences.t: τοῦ ὅ γ’ ἐπιμνησθεὶς ἔπεα πτερόεντ’ ἀγόρευεν·
sentences.tr: tou ho g’ epimnēstheis epea pteroent’ agoreuen·
sentences.l: Of him he, mindful, winged words spoke:
sentences.i: Mindful of him, he spoke winged words:
sentences.n: τοῦ ... ἐπιμνησθείς repeats the exact construction of 1.31, τοῦ ὅ γ’ ἐπιμνησθεὶς — the aorist passive participle of ἐπιμιμνήσκομαι with a genitive. ἔπεα πτερόεντα is the house table's fixed 'winged words'; the verb here is ἀγόρευεν, from ἀγορεύω, 'speak out, declare' (properly of assembly-speech), rather than the table's προσηύδα, so the fixed noun-phrase is kept while the verb is allowed to vary as Homer's own text varies it. ἀγόρευεν is unaugmented (Attic ἠγόρευεν).

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη, περὶ μέν σε βροτῶν πεπνυμένον εἶναι
Νέστωρ φάσχ’ ὁ γέρων, ὅτ’ ἐπιμνησαίμεθα σεῖο
οἷσιν ἐνὶ μεγάροισι, καὶ ἀλλήλους ἐρέοιμεν.
sentences.tr:
Atreïdē, peri men se brotōn pepnymenon einai
Nestōr phasch’ ho gerōn, hot’ epimnēsaimetha seio
hoisin eni megaroisi, kai allēlous ereoimen.
sentences.l:
“Son of Atreus, that beyond mortals you are prudent,
Nestor the old man used to say, whenever we called you to mind,
in his own halls, and questioned one another.
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, Nestor the old man used to say that you were prudent beyond other men, whenever we brought you to mind in his halls and questioned each other about you.
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδη is vocative, addressing Menelaus by the bare patronymic, as at 4.156. φάσχ’ is φάσκε, an imperfect of φάσκω with iterative colour, 'used to say', elided before ὁ. ἐπιμνησαίμεθα and ἐρέοιμεν are optatives in a general/repeated past clause introduced by ὅτε, 'whenever' — the regular Homeric construction for a customary past action. οἷσιν is the possessive ὅς, ἥ, ὅν, 'his own', referring to Nestor's halls at Pylos.

sentences.t: καὶ νῦν, εἴ τί που ἔστι, πίθοιό μοι·
sentences.tr: kai nyn, ei ti pou esti, pithoio moi·
sentences.l: And now, if it is possible somehow, do you heed me;
sentences.i: And now, if it is possible at all, listen to me;
sentences.n: πίθοιό is an aorist optative of πείθω (middle, 'obey, heed'), used as a polite request, with μοι the dative object. εἴ τί που ἔστι, 'if there is some way', is a softening parenthetical idiom. This opens the second half of Peisistratus's speech, turning from Menelaus's reputation for prudence to a practical plea about the grief at hand.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἐγώ γε
τέρπομ’ ὀδυρόμενος μεταδόρπιος, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἠὼς
ἔσσεται ἠριγένεια·
sentences.tr:
ou gar egō ge
terpom’ odyromenos metadorpios, alla kai ēōs
essetai ērigeneia·
sentences.i: for I myself find no pleasure in mourning after our meal — and besides, there will be an early dawn too;
sentences.n: τέρπομ’ ὀδυρόμενος μεταδόρπιος, literally 'I delight, lamenting, after-supper', sets the participle ὀδυρόμενος against τέρπομαι, 'take pleasure', in a near-oxymoron: Peisistratus states plainly he feels no such pleasure. μεταδόρπιος, 'after supper', is a rare compound adjective used predicatively. ἠριγένεια, 'early-born', is the fixed epithet of Dawn from the house table's whole-line formula ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς, though only the epithet itself appears here, standing for the goddess.

sentences.t:
νεμεσσῶμαί γε μὲν οὐδὲν
κλαίειν ὅς κε θάνῃσι βροτῶν καὶ πότμον ἐπίσπῃ.
sentences.tr:
nemessōmai ge men ouden
klaiein hos ke thanēisi brotōn kai potmon epispēi.
sentences.l:
yet I feel no resentment at all
at weeping for whoever of mortals dies and meets his fate.
sentences.i: yet I think it no shame at all to weep for any mortal who dies and meets his fate.
sentences.n: νεμεσσῶμαι, from the same root as νεμεσσᾶται at 4.158, here means 'feel indignation, take it amiss', with οὐδέν, 'not at all'. θάνῃσι is a subjunctive with the ending -ῃσι (Attic θάνῃ) in a general relative clause with κε (= ἄν). ἐπίσπῃ is the aorist subjunctive of ἐφέπω, 'come upon, meet with' (a fate); πότμος, 'fate, doom', is a near-synonym of μοῖρα and θάνατος already met earlier in this part.

sentences.t:
τοῦτό νυ καὶ γέρας οἶον ὀιζυροῖσι βροτοῖσιν,
κείρασθαί τε κόμην βαλέειν τ’ ἀπὸ δάκρυ παρειῶν.
sentences.tr:
touto ny kai geras oion oizyroisi brotoisin,
keirasthai te komēn baleein t’ apo dakry pareiōn.
sentences.l:
This now is indeed the sole due for wretched mortals,
to cut off one's hair, and to let a tear fall from one's cheeks.
sentences.i: This is indeed the one honor left to wretched mortals: to cut off their hair, and to let a tear fall from their cheeks.
sentences.n: γέρας, 'privilege, due, honour' — properly the portion belonging by right to someone, as a king's share of spoils — is used here with heavy irony: the only γέρας left to unhappy mortals in the face of death is the ritual of mourning itself. οἶον is 'alone, only' (smooth breathing). κείρασθαι and βαλέειν are epexegetic infinitives explaining γέρας: cutting the hair and letting tears fall (ἀπὸ ... βαλεῖν, with ἀπό governing παρειῶν, 'from the cheeks') were standard Greek gestures of mourning, the shorn lock often dedicated to the dead.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ ἐμὸς τέθνηκεν ἀδελφεός, οὔ τι κάκιστος
Ἀργείων·
sentences.tr:
kai gar emos tethnēken adelpheos, ou ti kakistos
Argeiōn·
sentences.l:
For indeed my own brother has died,
by no means the worst of the Argives;
sentences.i: For my own brother, too, has died — by no means the worst of the Argives;
sentences.n: τέθνηκεν is the perfect of θνῄσκω, 'has died', stressing the lasting state rather than the past event. ἀδελφεός is the epic/Ionic form of ἀδελφός. οὔ τι κάκιστος is litotes ('not at all the worst'), a typically Homeric understatement of Antilochus's excellence. This is the first point at which the Antilochus of 4.187 is named as Peisistratus's own brother.

sentences.t: μέλλεις δὲ σὺ ἴδμεναι·
sentences.tr: melleis de sy idmenai·
sentences.l: and you are likely to know it;
sentences.i: and you must know as much;
sentences.n: μέλλω + infinitive here carries its common Homeric sense 'be likely to, be bound to', rather than pure futurity: 'you must already know this'. ἴδμεναι is the perfect infinitive of οἶδα (Attic εἰδέναι), 'to know', built on the same stem as ἴδμεν at 4.138.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἐγώ γε
ἤντησ’ οὐδὲ ἴδον·
sentences.tr:
ou gar egō ge
ēntēs’ oude idon·
sentences.l:
for I myself
neither met him nor saw him;
sentences.i: for I myself never met him or saw him;
sentences.n: ἤντησα is the aorist of ἀντάω/ἀντιάω, 'meet, encounter' (+ genitive, here left understood, 'him'). ἴδον is the unaugmented aorist of ὁράω (= εἶδον). γε underscores ἐγώ, 'I myself, for my part': Peisistratus implies he was too young to have known Antilochus at Troy.

sentences.t:
περὶ δ’ ἄλλων φασὶ γενέσθαι
Ἀντίλοχον, πέρι μὲν θείειν ταχὺν ἠδὲ μαχητήν.
sentences.tr:
peri d’ allōn phasi genesthai
Antilochon, peri men theiein tachyn ēde machētēn.
sentences.l:
but beyond others, they say, Antilochus was,
exceedingly swift to run, and a fighter.”
sentences.i: but they say Antilochus surpassed the rest — outstandingly swift on his feet, and a fighter too.”
sentences.n: περὶ ... γενέσθαι and πέρι ... θείειν both use περί adverbially, 'exceedingly, beyond others', but only the second shows anastrophe (the accent thrown back to πέρι in its predicative, non-prepositional use before the infinitive); περὶ δ’ ... γενέσθαι keeps the ordinary accent; the word is used twice in close succession for emphasis. θείειν is the epic infinitive of θέω, 'run' (Attic θεῖν). μαχητής, 'fighter, warrior', is a rare noun beside the more common epithets of this type. This closes Peisistratus's speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη ξανθὸς Μενέλαος·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē xanthos Menelaos·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed fair-haired Menelaus:
sentences.i: In answer fair-haired Menelaus said to him:
sentences.n: The third and final use in this part of the fixed reply-formula τὸν/τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη ξανθὸς Μενέλαος (cf. 4.147, 4.168). Each time it introduces a reply to a different speaker in turn — Helen, then Peisistratus, then Peisistratus again. This is narration, not the speech itself; the mark and opening quotation mark belong on the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλ’, ἐπεὶ τόσα εἶπες, ὅσ’ ἂν πεπνυμένος ἀνὴρ
εἴποι καὶ ῥέξειε, καὶ ὃς προγενέστερος εἴη·
sentences.tr:
ō phil’, epei tosa eipes, hos’ an pepnymenos anēr
eipoi kai rhexeie, kai hos progenesteros eiē·
sentences.l:
“O friend, since you have said as much as a prudent man
would say and do, even one who might be older-born;
sentences.i: “Friend, since you have said as much as a prudent man would say and do, even one older than yourself;
sentences.n: ὦ φίλ’ is the house table's fixed vocative pattern. ὅσ’ ἂν ... εἴποι καὶ ῥέξειε is a relative clause of comparison with ἄν + optative, a potential construction, 'as much as a prudent man might say and do'. προγενέστερος is a comparative, 'born earlier, older' — Menelaus praises the young Peisistratus's words as fit for a man with more years behind him.

sentences.t:
τοίου γὰρ καὶ πατρός, ὃ καὶ πεπνυμένα βάζεις,
ῥεῖα δ’ ἀρίγνωτος γόνος ἀνέρος ᾧ τε Κρονίων
ὄλβον ἐπικλώσῃ γαμέοντί τε γεινομένῳ τε,
sentences.tr:
toiou gar kai patros, ho kai pepnymena bazeis,
rheia d’ arignōtos gonos aneros hōi te Kroniōn
olbon epiklōsēi gameonti te geinomenōi te,
sentences.i: for you have a father like that, since you speak prudent things too, and the offspring of a man for whom the son of Cronus spins good fortune, both at his marriage and at his birth, are easily recognized,
sentences.n: τοίου ... πατρός depends on an unexpressed ἐσσί, 'you are (of such a father)', a common Homeric ellipsis of the copula. βάζεις, 'chatter, talk', a fairly neutral verb of speaking, is here qualified by πεπνυμένα, 'prudent things' — the same fixed 'prudent' as πεπνυμένος elsewhere in this part, now generalized beyond Telemachus. ἀρίγνωτος, 'easily recognized' (ἀρι- intensive + γιγνώσκω), is a nominative predicate adjective agreeing with γόνος, 'offspring', which itself governs the genitive ἀνέρος, 'of a man'. Κρονίων, 'son of Cronus', is Zeus; γαμέοντι and γεινομένῳ are datives of a man's two life-moments, marriage and birth, both governed by ᾧ.

sentences.t:
ὡς νῦν Νέστορι δῶκε διαμπερὲς ἤματα πάντα
αὐτὸν μὲν λιπαρῶς γηρασκέμεν ἐν μεγάροισιν,
υἱέας αὖ πινυτούς τε καὶ ἔγχεσιν εἶναι ἀρίστους.
sentences.tr:
hōs nyn Nestori dōke diamperes ēmata panta
auton men liparōs gēraskemen en megaroisin,
huieas au pinytous te kai enchesin einai aristous.
sentences.l:
as now to Nestor he has granted, continually, all his days,
himself to grow old comfortably in his halls,
and his sons in turn to be prudent, and best with the spear.
sentences.i: as now he has granted to Nestor, all his days through, that he himself should grow old in comfort in his halls, and that his sons in turn should be sensible, and the best with the spear.
sentences.n: διαμπερὲς ἤματα πάντα, 'continually, through all his days', doubles the sense of unbroken duration. γηρασκέμεν is an epic infinitive in -έμεν of γηράσκω. λιπαρῶς, 'sleekly, comfortably', properly of a well-oiled, glossy condition, is here transferred to an easy old age. πινυτός, 'sensible, of sound mind', is a near-synonym of πεπνυμένος, from the same root πνυ-. ἔγχεσιν is a dative of respect with ἀρίστους, 'best with spears' — Nestor's sons Antilochus and Thrasymedes were noted fighters (cf. 3.442, 3.448).

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς δὲ κλαυθμὸν μὲν ἐάσομεν, ὃς πρὶν ἐτύχθη,
δόρπου δ’ ἐξαῦτις μνησώμεθα, χερσὶ δ’ ἐφ’ ὕδωρ
χευάντων.
sentences.tr:
hēmeis de klauthmon men easomen, hos prin etychthē,
dorpou d’ exautis mnēsōmetha, chersi d’ eph’ hydōr
cheuantōn.
sentences.l:
But let us set aside the weeping that came before,
and let us turn our minds again to supper, and over our hands
let them pour water.
sentences.i: But let us set aside the weeping that has already been done, and let us turn our minds again to supper, and let them pour water over our hands.
sentences.n: ἐάσομεν and μνησώμεθα are both hortatory in force (the first a future indicative used hortatively, the second a true subjunctive), 'let us leave off ... let us turn to'. ἐτύχθη is the aorist passive of τεύχω, 'came about, took place', used impersonally of the weeping now finished. χευάντων is a third-person plural imperative (aorist of χέω, 'pour'), addressed to the unnamed attendants, 'let them pour'. This begins Menelaus's practical turn from mourning to hospitality, resolving the grief that opened this part at 4.113.

sentences.t:
μῦθοι δὲ καὶ ἠῶθέν περ ἔσονται
Τηλεμάχῳ καὶ ἐμοὶ διαειπέμεν ἀλλήλοισιν.
sentences.tr:
mythoi de kai ēōthen per esontai
Tēlemachōi kai emoi diaeipemen allēloisin.
sentences.l:
and there will be words, even at dawn,
for Telemachus and me, to speak to one another.”
sentences.i: and there will be time, even at dawn, for Telemachus and me to talk things over with each other.”
sentences.n: ἠῶθεν, 'from dawn, at dawn', with the intensive περ, 'even at dawn', promises there will be time enough for talk the next morning too. διαειπέμεν is an epic infinitive in -έμεν, 'discuss thoroughly', epexegetic with μῦθοι ἔσονται, 'there will be words to be spoken'. ἀλλήλοισιν is the reciprocal pronoun, dative plural, epic -οισιν. Menelaus defers the real business of the visit — news of Odysseus — to the next day, closing his speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, Ἀσφαλίων δ’ ἄρ’ ὕδωρ ἐπὶ χεῖρας ἔχευεν,
ὀτρηρὸς θεράπων Μενελάου κυδαλίμοιο.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephat’, Asphaliōn d’ ar’ hydōr epi cheiras echeuen,
otrēros therapōn Menelaou kydalimoio.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Asphalion then poured water over their hands,
the brisk attendant of Menelaus, glorious.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Asphalion then poured water over their hands — the brisk attendant of glorious Menelaus.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ is a shorter, elided variant of the fixed ὣς φάτο, closing Menelaus's speech. ἔχευεν is the aorist of χέω, 'pour'. ὀτρηρὸς θεράπων and Μενελάου κυδαλίμοιο are both house-table renderings, 'brisk attendant' and 'of Menelaus, glorious', already fixed (in odyssey-014) at 4.23. This line, 4.217, repeats that same Greek line verbatim (see packet notes), and its English matches the wording already shipped there. A new named attendant, Asphalion, appears here for the first time, distinct from Eteoneus at 4.22.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ ἐπ’ ὀνείαθ’ ἑτοῖμα προκείμενα χεῖρας ἴαλλον.
sentences.tr: hoi d’ ep’ oneiath’ hetoima prokeimena cheiras iallon.
sentences.l: And they to the good things ready and set before them put out their hands.
sentences.i: And they put out their hands to the good things lying ready before them.
sentences.n: This line is identical to 2.149 from the already-published odyssey-002 (see packet notes), and its English here reproduces that shipped wording exactly, as required. ὀνείατα, 'good things', i.e. food, is from ὄνησις 'benefit'; προκείμενα is the present participle of πρόκειμαι, 'lie set out before one'; ἴαλλον is unaugmented, from ἰάλλω, 'send forth, put out (a hand)'. This closes the part with the company turning, after all the grief, to the meal Menelaus proposed at 4.212–213.
